newsitem.title: TURKEY: USDA says US-Turkey wheat row may be settled soon.
newsitem.headline: USDA says US-Turkey wheat row may be settled soon.

text.p: Turkey and the United States are close to agreeing to resolve issues that have been virtually banning U.S. wheat and other grain sales to Turkey in the past month, an official from the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) said on Monday.

"We have had very fruitful talks with Turkish officials and we are near agreeing mutually...in the next day or two," said Jonathan Jones, national export programme manager for USDA's Animal Plant and Health Inspection Service.

"There are no major differences, we are optimistic. If we agree we'll begin certifying sales to Turkey," he told a news briefing jointly held with other U.S. officials after a first day of talks with Turkish farm ministry officials in Ankara.

His remarks came a few hours after a senior Turkish farm official said Turkey would temporarily ease its strict health clearance requirements for several diseases in its wheat imports, especially those from its main grain supplier, the United States.

Muammer Yasarbas, deputy general manager of the Protection and Quarantine Directorate of the agricultural ministry, said the government would not seek clearances for five grain diseases and would impose a 0.05-percent tolerance for two others.
"Only a requirement of 0.05 percent will be sought in karnal bunt and ergot fungi," he told a seminar in Ankara on wheat quality arranged by the U.S. Wheat Associates.
"For five other diseases no clearance will be sought for a temporary period of time," he said.
Roy Barrett, marketing specialist with USDA's Foreign Agriculture Service, told the seminar earlier in the day that USDA believed ergot fungus was "more of a quality issue than a quarantine issue."
Turkey and the U.S. have been in disagreement since October, when Ankara held several U.S.-origin wheat cargoes for inspection against ergot fungus under its then zero-tolerance policy.
The U.S. responded by suspending phytosanitary certificates for grain exports to Turkey, virtually halting all grain sales.
Yasarbas said the new regulation would come out soon after members of the cabinet approved it, but added, "It is now in practice because we got verbal order from the agriculture minister."
Jones said two ships with an unspecified amount of U.S. wheat aboard were issued phytosanitary certificates by USDA last Friday and were being unloaded at Turkish ports.
Yasarbas said all U.S. wheat arriving at Turkey since the dispute began last month had been found clear in terms of ergot fungus according to the new regulation.
